But he who is a god to everyone else is certainly a man to himself, whether he wishes or not. He does not deceive his own conscience, even if he deceives someone else's.

Even princes and kings are shamefully courted with false flattery—not as great and chosen men, as is proper, but as gods. Yet honor is more truly given to a distinguished man, and love is more sweetly offered to a good one. So people call their deity by name, kneel before their images, and implore their genius, that is, their demon. And they think it safer to swear falsely by the genius of Jupiter than by the king.

We neither worship crosses nor wish for them. You, however, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps adore wooden crosses as parts of your gods. For what else are your standards, banners, and camp flags but crosses gilded and decorated? Your victorious trophies imitate not only the shape of a simple cross, but also of a man nailed to it.

We certainly see the sign of the cross naturally in a ship when it sails with swelling sails and glides along with outspread oar-blades. And when a yoke is lifted up, it is the sign of the cross; and when a man worships God with pure mind and outstretched hands. Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your own religion is shaped by it.
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians worship a crucified criminal, and he now turns the charge of cross-worship back onto pagan practice.

title: Christian innocence of infant blood and pagan blood-rites
english: Now I would like to meet the man who says or believes that we are initiated with the slaughter of an infant and with its blood. Do you think it possible that so soft, so tiny a body could receive the blows of wounds? That anyone could kill, pour out, and drain the fresh blood of a new and scarcely yet human being? No one can believe this except one who could dare to do it.

For I see that you expose your own children to wild beasts and birds, or strangle them and crush them out with a wretched kind of death. There are women who, by drinking drugs, extinguish the origin of a future human being in their very womb, and commit parricide before they give birth.

And these practices certainly descend from the teaching of your gods: for Saturn did not expose his sons, but devoured them. Rightly were infants sacrificed to him by parents in some parts of Africa, with caresses and a kiss suppressing their crying, so that a weeping victim might not be sacrificed.

The Taurians of Pontus and the Egyptian king Busiris had the rite of sacrificing guests; the Gauls slaughtered human or inhuman victims to Mercury; the Romans crushed alive a Greek man and a Greek woman, a Gallic man and a Gallic woman, in place of sacrifice; and to this day Jupiter Latiaris is worshipped by them with homicide, and, what is worthy of Saturn's son, he is fed with the blood of a wicked and criminal man.

I believe this same superstition taught Catiline the practice of conspiring under a covenant of blood, and taught Bellona to steep her sacred rite in a draught of human gore, and how to cure epilepsy with human blood, that is, with a heavier disease.

Not unlike them are those who devour wild beasts from the arena, smeared and stained with blood or with the limbs and entrails of a human being. For us it is not lawful even to see or hear of homicide, and so far do we keep away from human blood that we do not even know the blood of animals among our food.
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians are initiated by killing an infant and drinking its blood, and he turns the charge back onto pagan practices.

title: The incest slander is a demonic lie; pagan nations practice it, Christians keep chastity
english: And about the incestuous banquet, the gathering of demons has invented a great story against us. They wanted to stain the glory of our chastity by sprinkling it with shameful infamy, and to turn people away from us through terror of an unspeakable rumor before the truth could be examined.
So about this matter your Fronto too did not give testimony as one who affirms the charge. Rather, as an orator he sprinkled abuse. For these things were born rather from your own nations.

Among the Persians it is lawful to have intercourse with mothers. Among the Egyptians and Athenians marriages with sisters are legitimate. Your histories and tragedies glory in incests, which you gladly both read and hear. So you also worship incestuous gods, joined with mother, with daughter, with sister.

Rightly therefore incest is often detected among you, and always committed. Even without knowing it, wretched people, you can rush headlong into forbidden acts. While you scatter your lust for Venus promiscuously, while you sow children everywhere, while you frequently expose even children born at home to the mercy of strangers, you must of necessity run back upon your own, and stray into your own children. So you weave the story of incest even when you are unaware of it.

But we display modesty not by face but by mind. We gladly cling to the bond of one marriage. For the desire of procreation we know either one wife or none. We cultivate banquets that are not only chaste but also sober, for we do not indulge in feasts or prolong the banquet with wine, but we temper cheerfulness with seriousness. With chaste speech and a body more chaste still, many of us enjoy rather than boast of the perpetual virginity of an inviolate body. So far is the desire of incest from us that for some even a chaste union is a cause of shame.

And we do not consist of the lowest dregs of the people if we refuse your honors and purple robes. Nor are we seditious if we all understand one good, gathered together in the same quiet as individuals. Nor are we chatterers in corners if you are either ashamed or afraid to hear us publicly.
And that our number grows daily is not a crime of error but a testimony of praise. For in a beautiful manner of living, the native both stands firm and perseveres, and the outsider grows.

So finally we easily recognize one another not by a mark on the body, as you think, but by the sign of innocence and modesty. So we love one another with mutual love, which you resent, because we have not learned to hate. So we call one another brothers, which you begrudge, as people of one God the parent, as sharers in faith, as co-heirs of hope. For you do not recognize one another, and you rage in mutual hatreds, and you only acknowledge brothers indeed for parricide.
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians practice incest at their feasts, and he turns the charge back onto pagan myths and customs.

title: God cannot be housed or seen, yet is present everywhere
english: But do you think we hide what we worship because we have no shrines and altars? What idol could I fashion for God, when, if you judge rightly, man himself is God's idol? What temple could I build for him, when this whole world, made by his work, cannot contain him? And when I, a man, live in a wide space, should I confine the power of such majesty within one little shrine?

Is it not better to dedicate him in our mind? No, to consecrate him in our heart? Should I offer God victims and sacrifices, which he brought forth for my use, so that I throw his own gift back at him? That is ungrateful, when a good spirit and a pure mind and a sincere conscience are a pleasing victim.

So whoever cultivates innocence prays to God; whoever cultivates justice offers to God; whoever refrains from fraud appeases God; whoever rescues a person from danger slaughters a rich victim. These are our sacrifices, these are God's sacred rites: among us, the more just a person is, the more religious he is.

But the God we worship, you say, we neither show nor see. On the contrary, we believe God for this very reason: that we can perceive him, but cannot see him. For in his works and in all the movements of the world we behold his power always present, when it thunders, lightens, flashes lightning, when it clears.

Do not be surprised if you do not see God: wind and blasts drive, shake, and stir everything, and yet wind and blast do not come before the eyes. Even the sun, which is the cause of seeing for everyone, we cannot look at: our gaze is driven back by its rays, the viewer's sight is dulled, and if you look too long, all vision is extinguished.

What then? Could you endure the very maker of the sun, that source of light, when you turn away from his brilliance and hide from his lightning bolts? You want to see God with fleshly eyes, when you cannot even look at or grasp your own soul, by which you are given life and speech.

But, you say, God does not know human action, and established in heaven he cannot either visit everyone or know individuals. You err, O man, and you are deceived: for how is God far away, when all things heavenly and earthly, and those beyond this province of the world, are full of God? Everywhere he is not only near to us, but poured into us.
Look again at the sun: it is fixed in the sky, but it is spread over all lands; equally present everywhere, it is involved in and mingled with all things, and nowhere is its brightness violated.

How much more God, the author of all and watcher of all, from whom nothing can be hidden, is present in darkness, present in our thoughts, which are like another darkness! We do not merely act under him, but, I might almost say, we live with him.
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians have no temples, altars, or visible god, by arguing that the true God is worshiped in the mind and is known through his works and presence everywhere.

title: God's knowledge of all peoples and the Jews' desertion
english: Nor should we flatter ourselves about our numbers. We seem many to ourselves, but to God we are quite few. We divide the world into peoples and nations, but to God this whole world is one house. Kings learn the state of their kingdom through the varied services of their ministers, but God has no need of informers, for we live not only in his sight but in his bosom.

Yet it did the Jews no good that they too worshipped one God with altars and temples and the greatest superstition. You slip into ignorance if you remember only their earlier history and forget or never knew their later one.

For they too experienced our God, and he is the God of all. As long as they worshipped him purely, innocently, and religiously, as long as they obeyed his wholesome commands, from a few they became countless, from poor they became rich, from slaves they became kings. A small band overwhelmed many, unarmed men overwhelmed armed ones, fleeing men overwhelmed their pursuers, by God's command and with the elements assisting them.

Read their writings again, or if you prefer Roman authors, to pass over the ancients, consult Flavius Josephus or Antonius Julianus on the Jews. Then you will learn that their own wickedness earned them this fate, and that nothing happened to them that had not been foretold, if they persisted in their defiance.

So you will understand that they abandoned God before they were abandoned, and that they were not, as you impiously say, captured along with their God, but handed over by God as deserters from discipline.
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's attack on Christians, arguing that God knows all people without needing reports and that the Jews' misfortunes came from their own disobedience.

title: The world's end and the body's resurrection
english: As for the burning of the world, to refuse to believe that fire falls either unforeseen or with difficulty is a common error. Who among the wise doubts, who does not know, that everything which has arisen passes away, and everything which has been made is destroyed? The Stoics hold it as a settled opinion that the sky too, with everything contained in the sky, will pass into the force of fire just as it began, if the sweet water of the springs should cease to nourish the seas; because when the moisture is consumed, this whole world catches fire. The Epicureans hold the same view about the burning up of the elements and the ruin of the world. Plato speaks: he says that parts of the world are now flooded, now burn in alternating turns, and although he said that the world itself was made perpetual and indissoluble, he nevertheless added that for God its maker alone it is both dissoluble and mortal. So it is no wonder if this mass is destroyed by the one by whom it was built. You notice that the philosophers discuss the same things we say, not because we have followed in their footsteps, but because they have imitated the shadow of interpolated truth from the divine predictions of the prophets.

So also the more distinguished of the wise, Pythagoras first and chiefly Plato, handed down the condition of being reborn with a corrupted and halved faith: for when bodies are dissolved, they claim that souls alone remain forever and often pass over into other new bodies. To twist the truth, they add this too: that the souls of humans return into cattle, birds, and beasts. That view deserves not the serious study of a philosopher but the mockery of a mime. But for our purpose it is enough that even in this your wise men agree with us in some measure.

For who is so foolish or brutish as to dare to deny that a human being, since he could first be formed by God, can also be formed again? That there is nothing after death, and that there was nothing before birth? Just as it was possible to be born from nothing, so it is possible to be restored from nothing. Indeed, it is more difficult for what does not exist to begin than for what has existed to be repeated. Do you believe that anything is lost to God if it is withdrawn from our dull eyes? Every body, whether it dries into dust or dissolves into moisture or is pressed into ash or thinned into vapor, is withdrawn from us, but it is preserved for God, the guardian of the elements. Nor do we fear, as you believe, any loss from burial; rather, we practice the old and better custom of interment.

See, indeed, how all nature meditates on the resurrection that will be for our comfort. The sun sinks and is born again, the stars glide away and return, flowers die and revive, trees grow green again after old age, seeds do not grow green again unless they are corrupted: so the body in the tomb is like trees in winter: they hide their greenness with a pretended dryness. Why are you in a hurry for it to revive and return while winter is still raw? We must wait for the spring of the body as well. Nor am I unaware that many, conscious of their deserts, prefer to be nothing after death rather than to believe: they would rather be utterly extinguished than restored for punishment. Their error is increased both by the license allowed in this world and by God's great patience, whose judgment is the more just the slower it is.
orientation: Octavius is replying to Caecilius, arguing that even pagan philosophers agree the world will end by fire and that the body can be remade by God.

title: The eternal fire and the moral comparison of Christians with pagans
english: And yet people are warned by the books of the most learned men and by the poems of the poets about that river of fire and the burning heat that constantly surrounds the Stygian marsh. They have handed down that this fire is prepared for eternal torments, known both from the testimony of demons and from the oracles of the prophets.

That is why among them even King Jupiter himself swears religiously by the torrential banks and the black abyss. Foreknowing the punishment appointed for himself and his worshippers, he shudders at it.

Nor is there any limit or end to the torments. There the wise fire burns the limbs and restores them, tears them away and feeds them. Just as the fires of lightning touch bodies without consuming them, just as the fires of Mount Etna and Mount Vesuvius and of burning lands everywhere blaze without being spent, so that penal fire is not fed by the loss of what burns, but is nourished by the unending tearing of bodies.

But that those who do not know God are tormented as impious and unjust, no one deliberates unless he is profane, since to be ignorant of the parent and lord of all is no less a crime than to harm him.

And although ignorance of God is enough for punishment, just as knowledge avails for pardon, still if we Christians are compared with you, even though our discipline is inferior in some respects, we will nevertheless be found much better than you.

For you prohibit adulteries and commit them; we are born husbands solely for our wives. You punish crimes once committed; among us even to think of sin is to sin. You fear witnesses; we fear even our conscience alone, without which we cannot exist. Finally, the prison swarms with your number; no Christian is there unless he is accused of his religion or a fugitive.
orientation: Octavius is still replying to Caecilius, now describing the eternal punishment that awaits the wicked and then comparing Christian morals with pagan practice.

title: Fate, poverty, and God's testing
english: No one should seek comfort or excuse for his conduct in fate. Let a person's lot be whatever fortune wills, but the mind remains free, and so it is a man's action that is judged, not his station.

For what else is fate than what God has spoken concerning each one of us? Since he can know the material beforehand, he determines our fates according to the merits and qualities of each individual. Thus it is not our birth that is punished in us, but the nature of our character. And enough about fate, even if briefly for the present; we will discuss it more fully and completely another time.

As for the fact that most of us are called poor, that is not our disgrace but our glory. The mind is loosened by luxury, just as it is strengthened by frugality. And yet who can be poor if he lacks nothing, does not gape after another's goods, and is rich in God? That man is poorer who, though he has much, desires more.

I will tell you what I think: no one can be as poor as he was when he was born. Birds live without an inheritance and are fed day by day; and all these things were made for us, and if we do not covet them, we possess them.

Therefore, just as a man who travels a road is happier the lighter he walks, so in this journey of life the man is more blessed who lifts himself up by poverty and does not sigh under the burden of riches.

And yet if we thought wealth useful, we would ask it from God. Surely he to whom the whole belongs could grant us some portion. But we prefer to despise riches rather than to grasp them; we desire innocence more, we more urgently seek patience; we prefer to be good rather than extravagant.

And the human weaknesses of the body that we feel and suffer are not punishment; it is service as soldiers. For courage is strengthened in infirmities, and calamity is often the training ground of virtue. In fact, the powers of both mind and body grow sluggish without the exercise of labor. All your brave men, whom you praise as examples, flourished and became famous through their hardships.

So God both can help us and does not despise us, since he is the ruler of all things and the lover of his own. But in adversity he tests and examines each one; he weighs the character of individuals through dangers; he inquires into a man's will even to his final death, certain that nothing of his can perish. Therefore, as gold is proved by fire, so we are proved by critical moments.
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians are poor and miserable, explaining that fate is God's decree, poverty is no disgrace, and hardships are God's testing of his own.

title: The Christian as conqueror and the emptiness of worldly goods
english: What a beautiful sight for God when a Christian grapples with pain, when he stands arrayed against threats, punishments, and tortures, when, laughing, he drives home the din of death and the executioner's horror, when he raises his freedom against kings and rulers and yields only to God, whose he is, when he taunts the very man who pronounced sentence against him as a conqueror and victor!
For he has won who has obtained what he fought for.
What soldier would not court danger more boldly under his commander's eyes?
No one receives a reward before the test.
And yet a commander cannot give what he does not have: he cannot prolong life, but he can honor military service.
But God's soldier is neither abandoned in pain nor ended by death.
So a Christian can seem wretched, but he cannot be found wretched.
You yourselves carry calamitous men to heaven: Mucius Scaevola, who, having missed the king, would have perished among the enemy, had he not lost his right hand.
orientation: Octavius is still answering Caecilius, now showing that Christians endure torture as victors and that pagan wealth and rank are empty.

title: True freedom: rejecting pagan offerings, garlands, and philosophers
english: As for our contempt for the remnants of sacrifices and the cups that have been libated, this is not a confession of fear but an assertion of true freedom. For although everything that is born is an inviolable gift of God and is corrupted by no work of ours, we still abstain, lest anyone think that we either yield to the demons to whom the offering was made or are ashamed of our religion.

Who, after all, is there who doubts that we indulge ourselves in the flowers of spring, when we pluck the rose of spring and the lily and whatever else among the flowers has pleasing color and scent? For we use them both scattered, soft and loose, and woven into garlands around our necks. Indeed, forgive us for not crowning our heads: we are accustomed to draw the good breath of a flower with our nostrils, not to drink it in through the back of the head or the hair.

Nor do we crown the dead. In this matter I wonder at you all the more: how can you give the dead a torch if they can feel, or a crown if they feel nothing, when the blessed person has no need and the wretched person takes no joy in flowers?

But we adorn our funerals with the same tranquility with which we live, and we do not attach a withering crown, but from God we bear a living crown of eternal flowers. Quiet and modest, made secure by the generosity of our God, we animate our hope of future happiness by faith in his present majesty. Thus we both rise again in blessedness and already live by the contemplation of the future.

So let Socrates, the Atticus jester, look to it—he who confessed he knew nothing, yet boasted in the testimony of a most deceitful demon. Let Arcesilas too, and Carneades and Pyrrho and the whole crowd of Academics deliberate; let Simonides also postpone forever. We despise the arrogance of the philosophers, whom we know as corrupters and adulterers and tyrants, always eloquent against their own vices.

We, who display wisdom not in our dress but in our mind, do not speak great things but live them, and we glory that we have attained what they sought with the utmost effort and could not find. Why are we ungrateful? Why do we begrudge ourselves, if the truth of divinity has matured in the age of our time? Let us enjoy our good and temper our judgment of what is right: let superstition be restrained, let impiety be atoned for, let true religion be preserved.
orientation: Octavius is still answering Caecilius's charges against Christian customs, now explaining why Christians reject sacrificial food, garlands, and pagan philosophy.

title: The effect of Octavius's speech on the narrator
english: When Octavius had finished speaking, we sat stunned for some time, our faces fixed in silence. As for me, I was overcome by the sheer force of admiration. He had adorned what is easier to feel than to say with arguments, examples, and the authority of texts. He had turned back the malicious with the very weapons of the philosophers with which they arm themselves. And he had shown that truth is not only easy but also favorable.
orientation: Marcus the narrator describes the stunned silence that follows Octavius's closing speech, before Caecilius responds.

title: Caecilius concedes and the friends depart in joy
english: While I was turning these things over in silence, Caecilius burst out: "I congratulate my friend Octavius as much as I possibly can, and myself as well, and I do not wait for a verdict. We have won, and in this way: even shamelessly I claim the victory. For just as he is the victor over me, so I am the triumpher over error. And so, as far as the main question goes, I confess providence, I yield about God, and I agree about the sincerity of the sect, now ours. Even now, however, some things remain that do not obstruct the truth but are necessary for perfect instruction. Since the sun is already sinking toward evening, we will inquire into them more readily tomorrow, so that, being in agreement about the whole, we may inquire more promptly."

Then I said, "On behalf of all of us, I rejoice more fully that Octavius has also won for me, since the greatest envy of judging has been taken away from me. Yet I cannot repay his merit with words of praise: the testimony both of a man and of one man is weak. He has an extraordinary gift from God, by whom he was inspired to plead his case and, being helped, obtained it."
After this we parted, joyful and cheerful: Caecilius because he had believed, Octavius because he had won, and I because the one had believed and the other had won.
orientation: After Octavius's long defense, Caecilius interrupts the narrator's silent reflection to concede defeat, and the three friends agree to discuss remaining questions the next day.
